claims.text: Introducing controlled amounts of interstitial elements can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation in the high-entropy alloy.
Oxygen or nitrogen are candidate interstitial additions for the proposed intervention.
Interstitial oxygen and nitrogen promote solid-solution strengthening.
Interstitial additions inhibit deleterious phase segregation during thermal exposure.
Solid-solution strengthening reduces depletion of solute interstitials from the metal matrix.
Suppressing phase segregation and interstitial depletion maintains toughness after heating.
The intervention is expected to operate between 500°C and 800°C for exposures up to 100 hours.
The treated alloy will have at least 10% greater post-exposure toughness than the untreated baseline.
The baseline is an untreated alloy with the same composition and processing history.
The proposed loading boundary is tensile or compressive loading.
The required amount and preferred type of interstitial addition are not known.
Grain size and impurities may affect the post-exposure outcome.
The intervention can be tested by varying interstitial content, applying the specified heat treatment, and measuring toughness and microstructure.
Charpy impact testing or another standardized method will measure toughness, while microscopy will characterize the microstructure.
A treated-alloy toughness decrease of less than 5% relative to the untreated baseline is stated to falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Adding interstitial elements changes composition, whereas the baseline is required to have the same composition. The intended control should instead match the starting alloy and processing while differing only in interstitial content.
The loading boundary specifies tensile or compressive loading, but the primary proposed toughness measurement is Charpy impact testing, which is an impact-bending test outside that stated boundary.

The prediction requires at least a 10% toughness increase, but the falsification rule is phrased as a toughness decrease of less than 5%. That wording can describe little degradation, which may support rather than decisively falsify the central claim, and it does not cleanly test the stated 10% threshold.
